publications.title: Oxaliplatin-Based Versus Alkylating Agent in Neuroendocrine Tumors According to the O6-Methylguanine-DNA Methyltransferase Status: A Randomized Phase II Study (MGMT-NET).
publications.abstract_text: Alkylating agents (ALKY) are the main chemotherapies used for advanced neuroendocrine tumors (NETs). O 6 -Methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) status, as proficient (p) or deficient (d), may predict the response to ALKY.
publications.full_content: Full text links Cite Display options Display options Format Abstract PubMed PMID Abstract Purpose: Alkylating agents (ALKY) are the main chemotherapies used for advanced neuroendocrine tumors (NETs). O 6 -Methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) status, as proficient (p) or deficient (d), may predict the response to ALKY. Patients and methods: MGMT-NET (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03217097 ) was a phase II trial randomly assigning 1:1 for pMGMT or 2:1 for dMGMT-NETs to either ALKY or oxaliplatin (Ox). Inclusion criteria were a confirmed advanced pancreatic, thoracic, or unknown primary NETs with an indication for chemotherapy and tissue available. The primary aim was to detect a difference of 35% between the 3-month objective response rate (ORR) in pMGMT-NETs versus in dMGMT-NETs when treated with ALKY. A biomarker-stratified design was performed to compare ALKY and Ox in the dMGMT and pMGMT strata for the secondary end points. dMGMT was defined using pyrosequencing (PSQ; methylated MGMT ≥9%) and using immunochemistry ( H -score of MGMT <50) when PSQ was not interpretable. Results: From October 2018 to October 2021, 105 patients (55 pancreas, 38 thorax, 12 unknown) started either ALKY (n = 62) or Ox (n = 43). The median age was 63 years (range, 30-84), and 59% were males. NETs were G1 (19%), G2 (69%), or G3 (10%). Among patients with interpretable MGMT status, 56.9% (58 of 102) had a dMGMT-NET. The primary end point was not reached; the 3-month ORR was 10 (29.4%) versus 2 (8%), and the odds ratio was 3.5 (0.58-21.16), P = .172. However, best ORR (18 [52.9%] v 3 [11.5%]) and median progression-free survival (14.6 [95% CI, 7.2 to 22.1] v 11.3 [9.4 to 13.2] months) were higher for dMGMT-NETs versus pMGMT-NETs. MGMT status does not seem to affect the Ox efficacy. Conclusion: Despite the fact that the primary end point was not reached, ALKY has clinical activity in patients with dMGMT-NETs. evaluation.explanation: The study aligns well with the patient's diagnosis of a well-differentiated pancreatic NET (G1 included in the study population). While the patient currently has stable disease and might be considered for surgery or Somatostatin Analogues (SSAs) first, chemotherapy (e.g., streptozotocin or temozolomide) is a standard option for pancreatic NETs, particularly in neoadjuvant settings to downstage locally advanced tumors (vascular contact) or for future progressive disease. The study provides clinically actionable evidence (PMID: 39586038) demonstrating that MGMT deficiency predicts a significantly higher objective response rate to alkylating agents (52.9% vs 11.5% in proficient tumors), whereas oxaliplatin efficacy is independent of MGMT status. This evidence is highly relevant for the tumor board when discussing neoadjuvant strategies or selecting the most effective systemic chemotherapy regimen should the patient require cytoreduction.

relevant_trials.title: 177Lutetium-octreotate Treatment Prediction Using Multimodality Imaging in Refractory NETs
relevant_trials.brief_summary: The purpose of this study is to determine if 68Gallium-octreotate and 18Fluorodesoxyglucose uptake, apparent diffusion coefficient and post 177Lu-octreotate SPECT/CT dosimetry are reliable predictors for lesion-by-lesion treatment outcome.
relevant_trials.detailed_description:
This is a feasibility study evaluating the use of 177Lutetium-octreotate in the treatment of advanced refractory Neuroendocrine Tumors.

Objectives of the study:

1. Primary (on a lesion basis): To assess the value of the following parameters (obtained through functional and molecular imaging) for predicting the lesion-by-lesion PRRT treatment outcome:

   * 18FDG uptake on 18FDG PET/CT
   * 68Ga-octreotate uptake on 68Ga-octreotate PET/CT
   * Apparent diffusion coefficient on diffusion weighted MRI (for these 3 parameters, absolute values at baseline)
   * Tumor dosimetry on post 177Lu-octreotate SPECT/CT after each cycle.
2. Secondary (on a patient basis): To generate a patient-based response model based on the previously defined parameters.
3. Exploratory (on a lesion basis): To assess the value of the parameters mentioned in the primary objective for predicting the lesion-by-lesion PRRT treatment outcome:

   * absolute values of the three imaging parameters and their relative changes after each cycle;
   * serial tumor dosimetry on post-177Lu-octreotate SPECT/CT after each cycle.

Treatment will consist of 177Lu-octreotate injections in fixed activities of 7,4 GigaBecqurel each, given 11-13 weeks apart, injected intravenously with simultaneous infusion of an amino acid solution. (Before amino acid nephroprotection, ondansetron, methylprednisolone and metoclopramid, are given intravenously in order to prevent nausea or vomiting). Approximately 30 min after the beginning of the amino acid solution, 177Lu-octreotate is co-infused over 15-30 minutes. The amino acid infusion is continued at the same rate for 3-5 more hours (total infusion lasts 4-6 hours).

In total, 4 cycles (= injections of 177Lu-octreotate) are planned. However, the total number of administered cycles will be limited by critical organ (kidneys and bone marrow) threshold toxicities.

Treatment efficacy will be assessed:

* on a lesion-basis (change of longest transversal diameter).
* on a patient-basis using Response Evaluation Criteria In Solid Tumors (RECIST) 1.1.
relevant_trials.eligibility_criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

Patient-based:

1. Age above or equal to 18 years.
2. Histology-proven advanced GEP-NETs.
3. Disease progression defined as follows (at least one of the following):

   - Radiological disease progression (according to RECIST 1.1) on an MRI or CT over the last 12 months Or

   - Disease progression on a somatostatin receptor-imaging, PET/CT or SPECT/CT over the last 12 months \[apparition of new lesion(s) or increase in the transaxial plane diameter of more than 30% on the same imaging modality\] Or

   - Both of the following criteria (a+b):
   1. clinical progression:

      * sustained (for more than 2 weeks) increase of NET-specific hormonal hypersecretion related symptom frequency by 50% or,
      * sustained (for more than 2 weeks) increase of severity by 1 grade (according to NCI-CTCAE version 4.03).
   2. biochemical progression: by increase of NET-specific tumor markers (plasma Chromogranin A, plasma NSE, urine 5-HIAA or other) in two successive measurements.
4. Disease refractory to SSA's and/or standard systemic therapy available in Belgium at the time of inclusion criteria.
5. Long-acting SSAs should be discontinued at least 4 weeks before study treatment start date and, if needed, switched to short-acting analogues which should be stopped 48h before the treatment date.
6. Adequate renal function with GFR ≥ 50 mL/min/1.73m2 (evaluated by 51Cr-EDTA test).
7. Adequate bone marrow function with hemoglobin ≥ 9 g/dL; neutrophil ≥ 1.5·103/μL; platelet count ≥ 100·103/μL.
8. Adequate liver function with total bilirubin ≤ 2 x ULN and transaminases ≤ 5 x ULN, serum albumin \> 3 g/dL with normal prothrombin time (\> 70%).
9. ECOG Performance Status ≤ 1.
10. Women of childbearing potential and men with partners of childbearing potential must agree to use a highly-effective form of contraception for the duration of study participation and up to six months after the end of the treatment. A pregnancy test (serum) must be performed within 4 weeks prior to inclusion for every female patient of childbearing potential and it must be negative.
11. Patient's written informed consent obtained prior to any study procedure.
12. All necessary baseline procedures should be performed within 4 weeks prior to first 177Lu-octreotate injection (D0).

    Lesion-based:
13. The patient must have at least one target lesion fulfilling all of the below criteria:

    * On the 68Ga-octreotate PET/CT: tumor uptake higher than the physiological liver uptake (grade III or IV of the Rotterdam visual score) in a lesion with longest transaxial plane diameter ≥20mm (measured on the CT, part of the PET/CT);
    * At least one of these lesions morphologically measurable according to RECIST 1.1 and progressive on the MRI (or CT if MRI is not applicable);
    * Target lesion should not have been previously irradiated.

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Resectable tumor with curative intent.
2. Any major surgery within the last 6 weeks prior to inclusion in the study
3. Radiotherapy, chemotherapy, embolization, mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR)-inhibitors, receptor tyrosine-kinase inhibitors, interferon, or other investigational therapy within the last 12 weeks prior to inclusion in the study.
4. Diffuse bone marrow infiltration on the baseline 68Ga-octreotate PET/CT confirmed by MRI.
5. Prior external beam radiotherapy on kidneys or on more than 25% of bone marrow.
6. Patients with known uncontrolled brain metastases.
7. Patients with a significant medical, neuro-psychiatric, or surgical condition, currently uncontrolled by treatment, which, in the investigator's opinion, may interfere with completion of the study.
8. Pregnant or lactating patients.
9. Women of childbearing potential and men with partners of child-bearing potential refusing an adequate contraception.
relevant_trials.primary_outcome: The time to progression (TTP) for each target lesion assessed on MRI (or on CT scan if MRI is not possible).
relevant_trials.secondary_outcome: Best morphological response according to RECIST 1.1; Progression Free Survival; Biochemical response (evolution of NET-specific tumoral uptake).

publications.abstract_text: Our objective was to predict the outcome of peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) using multimodality imaging and tumor dosimetry on gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (GEP-NET) lesions and patients. Methods: This prospective study included patients with progressive GEP-NETs. Treatment consisted of 4 cycles of 7.4 GBq of 177 Lu-DOTATATE. Imaging parameters were measured on 68 Ga-DO...
publications.full_content: Full text links Cite Display options Display options Format Abstract PubMed PMID Abstract Our objective was to predict the outcome of peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) using multimodality imaging and tumor dosimetry on gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (GEP-NET) lesions and patients. Methods: This prospective study included patients with progressive GEP-NETs. Treatment consisted of 4 cycles of 7.4 GBq of 177 Lu-DOTATATE. Imaging parameters were measured on 68 Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT (SUV max/mean , somatostatin receptor [SSTR] tumor volume [TV], total lesion SSTR expression, and tumor-to-blood and tumor-to-spleen ratios), 18 F-FDG PET/CT (SUV max/mean , metabolically active TV, and total lesion glycolysis), and diffusion-weighted MRI (apparent diffusion coefficient) in a maximum of 5 target lesions per patient at approximately 10 wk after each injection. Tumor dosimetry was performed using SPECT/CT at 3 time points for every cycle. Baseline imaging parameters, their relative changes after PRRT cycle 1 (C1), and the tumor-absorbed dose at C1 were correlated with lesion morphologic outcome. The average values of the imaging parameters and the minimal, maximal, and mean C1 tumor-absorbed dose in each patient were tested for association with progression-free survival (PFS) and best objective response (RECIST 1.1). Results: In the 37 patients, the median PFS was 28 mo. Eleven of the 37 (30%) achieved a partial response (RECIST 1.1). After a median follow-up of 57 mo, the median time to lesion progression had not been reached in 84 morphologically evaluable lesions, with only 12 (14%) progressing (size increase ≥ 20% from baseline). Patients receiving a minimal C1 dose of 35 Gy in all target lesions exhibited a significantly longer PFS (48.1 vs. 26.2 mo; hazard ratio, 0.37; 95% CI, 0.17-0.82; P = 0.02). Volumetric 68 Ga-DOTATATE PET parameters correlated with lesion and patient outcome: patients with an SSTR TV decrease of more than 10% after C1 had a longer PFS (51.3 vs. 22.8 mo; hazard ratio, 0.35; 95% CI, 0.16-0.75; P = 0.003). There was no statistical evidence of an association between other dosimetric or imaging parameters and the lesion or patient outcome. Conclusion: Minimal tumor-absorbed dose at C1 is predictive of outcome in patients with GEP-NETs treated with PRRT, providing a basis for personalized dosimetry-guided treatment strategies. An SSTR TV decrease after C1 could be used for early therapy response assessment as a predictor of PRRT outcome. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01842165 . publications.title: 177 Lu-DOTATATE PRRT Safety and Organ-at-Risk Dosimetry in Patients With Gastroenteropancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors : Data From the Prospective Phase 2 LUMEN Study.
publications.abstract_text: The aim of this study was to assess the association among toxicity, dosimetry of organs-at-risk, and disease progression in patients with gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (GEP-NETs) treated with 177 Lu-DOTATATE.
publications.full_content: Full text links Cite Display options Display options Format Abstract PubMed PMID Abstract Purpose: The aim of this study was to assess the association among toxicity, dosimetry of organs-at-risk, and disease progression in patients with gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (GEP-NETs) treated with 177 Lu-DOTATATE. Patients and methods: Thirty-seven patients with GEP-NETs underwent 177 Lu-DOTATATE peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) in a single-arm, prospective, phase 2 study, where patients were followed up with blood tests, isotopic glomerular filtration rate (iGFR), and imaging examinations (CT/MRI and PET) every 6 months until disease progression. Adverse events (AEs) graded per CTCAEv4.03 and occurring during treatment were collected and followed up until resolution. Dosimetry, including biologically effective doses (BEDs) to kidneys, BED to bone marrow, and absorbed dose (AD) to spleen, was performed after each PRRT cycle. Statistical analyses explored associations among dosimetry, toxicity, and patient progression free-survival. Results: The most common AEs were anemia and lymphopenia (65%), followed by thrombocytopenia and fatigue (each 51%), alopecia (46%), and nausea (41%). The most common grade ≥3 AE was lymphopenia (43%). There was no grade ≥3 nephrotoxicity. The median iGFR % decrease was 11% ( P < 0.001), at a median follow-up of 23 months. iGFR %decrease and renal BED did not correlate (Spearman ρ = -0.09). Similarly, no significant association was found between bone marrow BED or spleen AD and the grades of hematological toxicities. We observed no association between progression free-survival and either the decline of renal function or the occurrence of hematological toxicities during PRRT. Conclusions: This study confirms the safety profile of 177 Lu-DOTATATE PRRT in patients with GEP-NETs irrespective of the dosimetry of organs at risk. Kidney, bone marrow, and spleen dosimetry measures were not associated with renal or hematological toxicity. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01842165 . publications.full_content: Full text links Cite Display options Display options Format Abstract PubMed PMID Abstract Background: Peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) with [ 177 Lu]Lu-DOTA-TATE has emerged as a promising treatment for gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (GEP-NETs). Its treatment protocol is currently standardised for all patients, resulting in different patient outcomes. This study investigates the variability of tumours and organs-at-risk (kidneys and red marrow) dosimetric parameters across treatment cycles in patients with pancreatic and intestinal NETs. Data from 37 patients enrolled in a prospective phase II study (LuMEn) were analysed. Treatment consisted of four cycles of [ 177 Lu]Lu-DOTA-TATE administered 8-12 weeks apart. Three-time-point SPECT/CT imaging was performed after each treatment cycle, and dosimetry of tumours and organs-at-risk (kidneys and red marrow) was conducted following the medical internal radiation dose formalism. Coefficients of variation (CoV) assessed the variability of absorbed doses, activity concentrations on day 1, and effective half-lives. Linear mixed effect models (SAS software) were used to investigate the evolution of the dosimetric parameters over cycles, discerning between different primary NET types and grades of tumours. Results: There is an important variability in absorbed doses and activity concentrations among patients, particularly in tumours (CoV: ~50%). Tumour absorbed doses and activity concentrations decreased over treatment cycles in pancreatic NETs, although at a limited rate (~-13%/cycle). An opposite trend was observed for the kidneys ( ~ + 8%/cycle). Effective half-lives remained relatively constant across cycles for both organs-at-risk and tumours. The primary NET type significantly influenced effective half-lives in tumours, shorter in pancreatic NETs than intestinal NETs (77 h vs. 107 h, p < 0.0001). No significant effect of the grade was observed on either of the variables investigated. Conclusions: Our study revealed considerable variations in tumour absorbed doses among patients with NETs treated with a standardized protocol. These findings confirm the need for personalized dosimetry approaches in PRRT, considering patient and tumour characteristics. Trial registration: EudraCT Number: 2012-003666-41. evaluation.explanation: This prospective Phase II study (LUMEN) provides meaningful clinical evidence to guide therapy recommendations for this patient. Biologically, the patient's SSTR-positive, G1 pancreatic NET aligns perfectly with the study population (advanced GEP-NETs). Clinically, the tumor board is weighing upfront resection versus neoadjuvant therapy to improve resectability of the locally advanced primary tumor. Although the patient currently has stable disease and the trial strictly enrolled progressive/refractory patients, the study's published objective response rate (30%) and progression-free survival (median 28 months) are critical data points for estimating the likelihood of tumor downstaging with PRRT in the neoadjuvant setting. Furthermore, the study's safety and dosimetry data inform the risk/benefit assessment for this treatment approach. The evidence is therefore directly transferable to the decision-making process regarding the utility of PRRT for this patient.

relevant_trials.title: Study of Pasireotide Long Acting Release (LAR) in Patients With Metastatic Neuroendocrine Tumors (NETs)
relevant_trials.brief_summary: The goal of this clinical research study is to learn if the study drug, Pasireotide LAR can shrink or slow the growth of Metastatic Neuroendocrine Carcinomas. The safety of this drug will also be studied. The patient's physical state, changes in the size of the tumor, and laboratory findings taken while on-study will help us decide if Pasireotide LAR is safe and effective.
relevant_trials.detailed_description:
This is a multi-institutional, prospective phase II open-label trial.

The investigational drug used in this study is pasireotide LAR 60 mg. Pasireotide will be administered as an intramuscular injection at the beginning of every cycle which is defined as 28 days (+/- 3 days). Study treatment should begin within 14 days following enrollment into the study and continue until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, or withdrawal of consent. Safety and efficacy will be assessed throughout the treatment period.
relevant_trials.eligibility_criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Locally unresectable or metastatic carcinoid or pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors
* Tumors must be considered well or moderately differentiated (or low to intermediate grade). Patients with poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinomas or small cell carcinomas are excluded from the study.
* No prior systemic antineoplastic neuroendocrine tumor treatment (including prior somatostatin analogs). However patients who have received a short course of subcutaneous (SQ) octreotide (\<10 days) in the past are eligible if \> 1 week has elapsed from their last octreotide injection.
* Minimum of four weeks since any major surgery
* Measureable disease by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST)
* Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status ≤1
* Life expectancy 12 weeks or more
* Adequate bone marrow function as shown by: absolute neutrophil count (ANC) ≥ 1.0 x 10\^9/L, Platelets ≥ 75 x 10\^9/L, hemoglobin (Hgb) \> 8 g/dL
* Adequate liver function as shown by: serum bilirubin ≤ 2.0 x upper limit of normal (ULN), and serum transaminases activity ≤ 2 x ULN, with the exception of serum transaminases (\< 3 x ULN) if the patient has liver metastases
* Adequate renal function as shown by serum creatinine ≤ 2.0 x ULN
* Fasting serum cholesterol ≤300 mg/dL OR ≤7.75 mmol/L AND fasting triglycerides ≤ 2.5 x ULN. Note: In case one or both of these thresholds are exceeded, the patient can only be included after initiation of appropriate lipid lowering medication.
* Women of childbearing potential (WOCBP) must have a negative serum pregnancy test within 14 days of the administration of the first study treatment. Women must not be lactating. Both men and WOCBP must be advised of the importance of using effective birth control measures during the course of the study.
* Signed informed consent to participate in the study must be obtained from patients after they have been fully informed of the nature and potential risks by the investigator (or his/her designee) with the aid of written information.

Exclusion Criteria:

* Uncontrolled brain or leptomeningeal metastases, including patients who continue to require glucocorticoids for brain or leptomeningeal metastases
* Patients with prior or concurrent malignancy except for the following: adequately treated basal cell or squamous cell skin cancer, or other adequately treated in situ cancer, or any other cancer from which the patient has been disease free for 5 years
* Patients with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus or a fasting plasma glucose \> 1.5 ULN or glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c) \>8%. Note: At the principle investigator's discretion, non-eligible patients can be re-screened after adequate medical therapy has been instituted.
* Patients with symptomatic cholelithiasis
* Patients who have congestive heart failure: New York Heart Association (NYHA) Class III or IV, unstable angina, or a history of acute myocardial infarction within the 6 months preceding enrollment
* Patients who have any severe and/or uncontrolled medical conditions or other conditions that could affect their participation in the study such as:

  * Severely impaired lung function
  * Any active (acute or chronic) or uncontrolled infection/ disorders
  * Nonmalignant medical illnesses that are uncontrolled or whose control may be jeopardized by the treatment with the study therapy
* Known hypersensitivity to somatostatin analogues or any component of the pasireotide LAR formulation
* Corrected QT interval (QTcF) of \>470 msec on screening Electrocardiogram (ECG)
* Risk factors for Torsades de Pointes such as cardiac failure, clinically significant/symptomatic bradycardia
* Clinically significant hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia that are not correctable
* History of sustained ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, advanced heart block, or idiopathic syncope thought to be related to ventricular arrhythmia
* Concomitant medication(s) known to increase the QT interval
* History of noncompliance to medical regimens or unwillingness to comply with the protocol

publications.full_content: Full text links Cite Display options Display options Format Abstract PubMed PMID Abstract Pasireotide long-acting repeatable (LAR) is a novel somatostatin analog (SSA) with avid binding affinity to somatostatin receptor subtypes 1, 2, 3 (SSTR1,2,3) and 5 (SSTR5). Results from preclinical studies indicate that pasireotide can inhibit neuroendocrine tumor (NET) growth more robustly than octreotide in vitro. This open-label, phase II study assessed the clinical activity of pasireotide in treatment-naïve patients with metastatic grade 1 or 2 NETs. Patients with metastatic pancreatic and extra-pancreatic NETs were treated with pasireotide LAR (60 mg every 4 weeks). Previous systemic therapy, including octreotide and lanreotide, was not permitted. Tumor assessments were performed every 3 months using Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) criteria. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS). The secondary endpoints included overall survival (OS), overall radiographic response rate (ORR), and safety. Twenty-nine patients were treated with pasireotide LAR (60 mg every 4 weeks) and 28 were evaluable for response. The median PFS was 11 months. The most favorable effect was observed in patients with low hepatic tumor burden, normal baseline chromogranin A, and high tumoral SSTR5 expression. Median OS has not been reached; the 30-month OS rate was 70%. The best radiographic response was partial response in one patient (4%), stable disease in 17 patients (60%), and progressive disease in ten patients (36%). Although grade 3/4 toxicities were rare, pasireotide LAR treatment was associated with a 79% rate of hyperglycemia including 14% grade 3 hyperglycemia. Although pasireotide appears to be an effective antiproliferative agent in the treatment of advanced NETs, the high incidence of hyperglycemia raises concerns regarding its suitability as a first-line systemic agent in unselected patients. SSTR5 expression is a potentially predictive biomarker for response. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01253161 . evaluation.explanation: The study provides meaningful clinical evidence for this patient, who presents with a metastatic, G1, SSTR-positive pancreatic NET and is a candidate for first-line systemic therapy. The study evaluates Pasireotide LAR, a somatostatin analog (SSA), in a treatment-naïve population with metastatic G1/G2 NETs, directly aligning with the patient's disease biology and clinical status (ECOG 0, stable but metastatic disease). While standard SSAs (octreotide/lanreotide) are typically first-line, this Phase II study offers specific evidence regarding the efficacy (median PFS 11 months) and safety profile of Pasireotide, particularly highlighting a high rate of hyperglycemia (79%). This evidence is clinically relevant for the tumor board to weigh the antiproliferative benefits of this broad-spectrum SSA against its metabolic toxicity profile when selecting the optimal SSA therapy.

relevant_trials.eligibility_criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Willing and able to provide written informed consent for the trial
* ≥ 18 years of age
* Histologically- or cytologically- confirmed locally advanced or metastatic WDNET
* SSA therapy is recommended by physician for disease management, and has not yet begun
* ECOG performance status of 0, 1, or 2

Exclusion Criteria:

* Currently participating in a study of an investigational agent
* Prior chemotherapy, targeted small molecule therapy within 2 weeks prior to study Day 1 or not recovered (i.e., ≤ Grade 1 or at baseline) from adverse events due to a previously administered agent

  \*Note: Subjects with ≤ Grade 2 neuropathy or ≤ Grade 2 alopecia are an exception to this criterion and may qualify for the study
* No concurrent chemotherapy or targeted small molecule therapy
* If received major surgery, not recovered adequately from the toxicity and/or complications from the intervention prior to starting the study
* Known additional malignancy that is progressing or requires active treatment
* Active infection requiring systemic therapy
* Known psychiatric or substance abuse disorders that would interfere with cooperation with the requirements of the trial

evaluation.explanation: This study is relevant because it addresses the choice between two standard-of-care Somatostatin Analogues (SSAs) for this patient's specific disease profile. 1) **Disease Alignment:** The patient has a well-differentiated (G1), SSTR-positive metastatic neuroendocrine tumor, which matches the study population of locally advanced or metastatic WDNETs. 2) **Treatment Context:** SSAs (Octreotide LAR or Lanreotide) are the guideline-recommended first-line systemic therapy for antiproliferative control in G1 pancreatic NETs, particularly if the patient is not an immediate candidate for curative surgery or requires disease stabilization. 3) **Evidence Quality:** While the study focuses on patient experience (pain scores, preference) rather than antitumor efficacy (Phase 4), this evidence is clinically actionable for decision-making. Since Octreotide and Lanreotide are often considered therapeutically similar, data regarding injection pain and patient preference (Raj et al., 2022) provides meaningful guidance for selecting the specific agent to optimize long-term adherence and quality of life in this chronic treatment setting.

all_evaluations.explanation: The study is not relevant because the disease biology does not align. The patient has a Grade 1 (Ki-67 2%) well-differentiated NET, whereas the study specifically enrolled patients with Grade 2-3 NETs (median Ki-67 35%) and explicitly excluded Grade 1 disease. Biologically, indolent G1 tumors are distinct from the higher-grade populations studied. Furthermore, the study investigated Avelumab (immunotherapy) in patients with progressive disease, showing no objective responses; immunotherapy is not a standard or typically considered experimental approach for stable G1 NETs, which are managed with SSAs, PRRT, or surgery. Consequently, negative results from a biologically distinct, higher-grade population do not provide actionable evidence for this patient's treatment decisions.

It is a general registry (ROOT) designed to collect real-world data and validate observational methodologies across various advanced malignancies, rather than a clinical trial evaluating the efficacy of a specific intervention for neuroendocrine tumors. The listed publications are methodological papers, reviews on next-generation sequencing, or focused on unrelated cancers (e.g., BRAF in colorectal cancer), containing no specific outcome data for pancreatic NETs. Consequently, the study fails to meet the criteria for Evidence Quality and Relevance, as it lacks actionable data on the comparative effectiveness of surgery, PRRT, or somatostatin analogs that is required to address the tumor board's question regarding the optimal management of this patient's G1 SSTR-positive PanNET.
all_evaluations.trial_title: The Registry of Oncology Outcomes Associated with Testing and Treatment

all_evaluations.explanation: This prospective observational study provides meaningful evidence for the patient's condition, meeting all criteria. Biologically, the patient's G1 well-differentiated pancreatic NET aligns perfectly with the study population, which included G1/G2 pancreatic NETs. Clinically, the patient is a strong candidate for Somatostatin Analog (SSA) therapy (Lanreotide) for antiproliferative control, given her SSTR-positive status and stable disease, consistent with ESMO/ENETS guidelines for non-functioning G1 PanNETs. The study provides specific, actionable real-world outcome data for this subgroup, reporting a 24-month progression-free survival (PFS) rate of 60.8% for pancreatic NETs. This evidence is directly relevant for informing the tumor board's decision-making regarding the expected durability of disease control with systemic SSA therapy versus surgical intervention or other approaches.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Community-based Neuroendocrine Tumor (NET) Research Study

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not meet the criteria for evidence quality and relevance to inform therapy recommendations. This is an observational study focused on validating biomarkers (circulating tumor cells and ctDNA) rather than evaluating the efficacy or safety of a therapeutic intervention. While the disease biology (Pancreatic NET) aligns with the patient's diagnosis, the study does not compare treatment outcomes or provide actionable data to guide the specific clinical decision between surgery, PRRT, or somatostatin analogs. Furthermore, the provided data indicates 'No detailed findings available' and lists background literature rather than trial-specific results demonstrating clinical utility. Consequently, the study offers no evidence to support a specific therapeutic recommendation for this patient.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Circulating Tumor Cells and Tumor DNA in HCC and NET

all_evaluations.explanation: The study evaluates minimally invasive pancreatic enucleation, a parenchyma-sparing surgical technique reserved for small, benign, or low-grade tumors without main duct involvement or nodal disease. While the patient has a low-grade PanNET (biology alignment), she presents with a large (4-5 cm) primary tumor causing main pancreatic duct dilation, vascular contact, and confirmed lymph node metastases. This clinical presentation mandates formal oncologic resection (pancreaticoduodenectomy) with lymphadenectomy rather than enucleation to ensure adequate margins and nodal clearance. Therefore, the study fails the Treatment Context criterion, as the specific surgical intervention investigated is clinically contraindicated for this patient's locally advanced and node-positive disease.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Minimally Invasive Pancreatic Enucleation With Main Pancreatic Duct Exposure, Repair or Reconstruction

all_evaluations.explanation: The study fails the evidence quality and relevance criterion. While the disease biology (SSTR-positive, well-differentiated GEP-NET) and treatment context (Lutathera) align with the patient's potential treatment path—specifically considering PRRT as a systemic or neoadjuvant option—the provided published results are limited to the study design and baseline characteristics (REAL-LU interim analysis). The publication explicitly states that effectiveness and safety analyses are anticipated as data mature. Without reported clinical outcomes such as progression-free survival, objective response rates, or toxicity profiles, this study does not currently provide actionable evidence to guide therapeutic decision-making for this patient.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Italian Prospective Observational Study Assessing the Effectiveness and Outcomes Associated With Lutathera Treatment in GEP-NETs

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not meet the criteria for clinical applicability or evidence relevance for this patient. The study evaluates postoperative pancreatic fistula specifically following minimally invasive enucleation (MIEN) for benign or low-grade tumors. While the patient has a G1 PanNET, her primary tumor is large (41x51x35 mm), located in the pancreatic head with vascular contact, and associated with metastatic disease. These anatomical and oncological characteristics require a formal oncological resection (pancreaticoduodenectomy/Whipple) rather than enucleation, which is typically reserved for small, localized lesions. The study explicitly excludes patients requiring standard oncological resection. Therefore, evidence regarding fistula rates and outcomes after enucleation is not transferable to the major resection this patient would require, nor does it inform the decision between surgery and systemic therapy.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Pancreatic Fistula After Minimally Invasive Enucleation

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not meet the criteria for clinical applicability or evidence relevance for this patient. The study (NCT06779708) is a diagnostic accuracy trial evaluating the role of intraoperative ultrasound (IOUS) specifically in patients classified as cM0 (non-metastatic) on preoperative imaging to detect occult liver metastases. The patient, however, presents with clinically evident metastatic disease (cM1) in the liver and lymph nodes confirmed by MRI and DOTATOC PET/CT. Consequently, the study's primary endpoint regarding the detection rate of occult metastases in a cM0 population does not address the patient's clinical need, which involves choosing between upfront resection of known disease versus neoadjuvant therapy. Furthermore, the provided publication data consists of background literature (dated 2010–2019) rather than results from this specific prospective study (conducted 2020–2023), offering no new actionable evidence to guide therapeutic decision-making.
all_evaluations.trial_title: The Role of Intraoperative Hepatic Ultrasonography in Gastrointestinal or Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumor

all_evaluations.explanation: The study aligns with the patient's tumor biology (SSTR-positive, G1/G2 GEP-NET) and evaluates a relevant intervention (PRRT). However, the provided published results (PMID: 39607652) focus exclusively on radiation dosimetry, external dose rates, and radiation protection guidelines for discharge planning. The publication does not report essential clinical outcomes such as Progression-Free Survival (PFS), Objective Response Rate (ORR), or patient-centered toxicity profiles necessary to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of 177Lu-oxodotreotide compared to Octreotide LAR. Without efficacy data, this study does not provide actionable evidence to inform the Tumorboard's decision regarding the selection of PRRT versus surgery or other systemic therapies for this patient.
all_evaluations.trial_title: A Study Comparing Treatment With Lutetium[177Lu] Oxodotreotide Injection to Octreotide LAR in Patients With GEP-NETs

all_evaluations.explanation: While the study aligns with the patient's disease biology (G1 GEP-NET) and treatment context (Lanreotide eligibility), it fails the evidence quality and relevance criterion for informing therapy recommendations. The OPERA study is a non-interventional, observational study focused on patient perception of information and quality of life (QLQ-INFO25) rather than therapeutic efficacy or safety outcomes. The published results demonstrate stability in information perception but do not provide data on tumor control, survival, or comparative effectiveness that would assist the tumor board in choosing between surgical resection, PRRT, or systemic SSA therapy for this patient's locally advanced/metastatic pancreatic NET.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Perception of Information and Quality of Life in Neuroendocrine Tumour on Lanreotide Autogel

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not provide meaningful evidence for this patient because the published results provided (PMID 37429302) are exclusively from the sarcoma cohort of this basket trial, containing no data on the neuroendocrine tumor (NET) cohort. Therefore, the criterion for Evidence Quality and Relevance is not met as there are no outcomes to apply to the patient's disease. Additionally, the study fails the Treatment Context criterion; the patient is at the initial stage of management with standard options available (surgery, SSAs, PRRT), whereas the study's NET cohort inclusion criteria required well-differentiated tumors to be refractory to four lines of prior treatment. Given the lack of NET-specific data in the provided results and the significant disparity between the patient's treatment-naive status and the study's refractory setting, this study cannot inform therapy recommendations.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Secured Access to Pembrolizumab for Patients With Selected Rare Cancer Types

all_evaluations.explanation: The COMPETE trial provides critical Phase 3 evidence relevant to this patient's care. Biologically, the patient matches the study population perfectly (G1, SSTR-positive PanNET). Although the patient currently has stable disease and the trial enrolled patients with progressive disease, the results demonstrating superior progression-free survival (23.9 vs 14.1 months) with 177Lu-edotreotide PRRT compared to Everolimus are highly applicable. This evidence informs the choice of systemic therapy should the patient be deemed unresectable or progress in the future. Furthermore, given the clinical consideration of neoadjuvant PRRT to facilitate R0 resection for this locally advanced/oligometastatic case, the study's confirmation of PRRT's robust efficacy supports its biological rationale in this setting. The evidence helps prioritize PRRT over mTOR inhibitors in the treatment algorithm for SSTR-positive GEP-NETs.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Efficacy and Safety of 177Lu-edotreotide PRRT in GEP-NET Patients

all_evaluations.explanation: The study aligns with the patient's disease biology (well-differentiated GEP-NET) and the potential clinical scenario of surgical resection. However, it fails the evidence relevance criterion for informing therapy recommendations. The study is designed to validate a biomarker (NETest) for monitoring surgical completeness and predicting recurrence, rather than evaluating the comparative efficacy or safety of a therapeutic intervention. While the patient is a candidate for surgery, the study results support the use of a diagnostic tool for post-operative surveillance rather than providing evidence to guide the primary therapeutic decision (e.g., choosing between upfront surgery, neoadjuvant PRRT, or systemic therapy). Therefore, it does not offer actionable insights to resolve the tumor board's question regarding the recommended therapy.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Surgical Intervention and the NETest

all_evaluations.explanation: The study fails the Disease/Biology Alignment criterion. The patient has a well-differentiated Grade 1 (Ki-67 2%) neuroendocrine tumor (NET) of the pancreas, whereas the study evaluates Nivolumab and Ipilimumab specifically in rare genitourinary (GU) malignancies, including a cohort for *high-grade* neuroendocrine carcinomas or small cell carcinomas of the GU tract. There is a fundamental biological disconnect between well-differentiated G1 pancreatic NETs (typically immunologically 'cold' and unresponsive to checkpoint inhibitors) and high-grade GU neuroendocrine carcinomas. Evidence from high-grade GU tumors cannot be clinically extrapolated to inform therapy for a G1 pancreatic NET, rendering the study results inapplicable to this patient's treatment planning.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Nivolumab Combined With Ipilimumab for Patients With Advanced Rare Genitourinary Tumors

all_evaluations.explanation: The study is not relevant for this patient. While the study evaluates entrectinib in solid tumors (including a published case of a responder with a neuroendocrine tumor) and the patient has a pancreatic NET, the intervention is strictly targeted at malignancies harboring *NTRK*, *ROS1*, or *ALK* gene fusions. The patient presents with a well-differentiated Grade 1 pancreatic NET with confirmed SSTR2 positivity, a biological profile where such fusions are exceptionally rare (<1%) and not documented in the provided clinical history. The patient’s disease biology strongly aligns with SSTR-targeted therapies (e.g., somatostatin analogs, PRRT) rather than tyrosine kinase inhibitors targeting these specific rare fusions. Without confirmation of an *NTRK*, *ROS1*, or *ALK* rearrangement, the study's evidence regarding entrectinib efficacy is not clinically applicable to this patient's treatment planning, as the requisite biological target is presumed absent.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Basket Study of Entrectinib (RXDX-101) for the Treatment of Patients With Solid Tumors Harboring NTRK 1/2/3 (Trk A/B/C), ROS1, or ALK Gene Rearrangements (Fusions)

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not provide meaningful evidence for this patient's treatment for two key reasons. First, the provided publication is a study protocol describing the design of the RETNET trial, but it does not report efficacy or safety results (Criterion 3 not met). Without published outcomes, the study cannot inform the choice between embolization modalities. Second, the treatment context is not applicable (Criterion 2 not met). The patient has stable, oligometastatic liver disease (two lesions ≤10 mm) and is being evaluated for curative-intent resection or ablation. The study targets patients with unresectable, liver-dominant, progressive, or symptomatic metastases requiring palliative embolization. Embolization is generally not indicated for such low-volume, stable disease where ablation or surgery is feasible.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Randomized Embolization Trial for NeuroEndocrine Tumor Metastases to the Liver

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not meet the Disease/Biology Alignment criterion. The patient has a Grade 1 well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor with a very low Ki-67 index (2%), whereas this study (NCT03079440) is specifically designed for patients with Grade 3 tumors (Ki-67 > 20%). While the intervention (Temozolomide/Capecitabine) is indeed used for well-differentiated G1/G2 pancreatic NETs, the clinical evidence generated by this specific trial focuses on its efficacy in the high-grade (G3) population, which has distinct biological behavior and chemosensitivity compared to the patient's indolent G1 disease. Consequently, the outcomes from this high-grade cohort cannot be reasonably extrapolated to inform treatment decisions for this Grade 1 patient, for whom other studies (e.g., ECOG E2211) provide the relevant evidence base.
all_evaluations.trial_title: TEMCAP in Grade 3 and Low Ki-67 Gastroenteropancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors

all_evaluations.explanation: This study does not provide meaningful evidence to guide therapy recommendations for this patient. While the disease biology (neuroendocrine tumors) broadly aligns, the study is a retrospective database (registry) rather than an interventional trial testing a specific treatment. The publications listed in the record are historical background references (e.g., epidemiology papers from 2008/2017, RECIST criteria, or pathology papers focusing on Grade 3/NEC) rather than results generated by this specific registry. Consequently, there is no novel prospective evidence regarding the efficacy or safety of interventions (such as resection, PRRT, or SSAs) that would inform the clinical decision between surgical and neoadjuvant approaches for this patient's G1 pancreatic NET.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Multicenter Retrospective Database on Prognostic and Predictive Factors in Patients With Neuroendocrine Tumors

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not provide meaningful clinical evidence for this patient. First, the provided publications are from unrelated trials (e.g., DESTINY-Breast03, KEYNOTE-042) or general design papers, not results from the ANTARES study itself; thus, there is no efficacy data to evaluate. Second, the biological alignment is poor: the patient has a Grade 1 well-differentiated PanNET, a tumor type that is typically immunologically 'cold' (low mutational burden, low PD-L1), making response to single-agent PD-1 blockade (Nivolumab) unlikely compared to standard therapies. Third, the clinical context does not match; the patient is treatment-naïve or stable under surveillance and has multiple established standard-of-care options (somatostatin analogs, PRRT, surgery) available. The study requires progression on approved therapies and high PD-L1 expression (CPS ≥ 10), neither of which applies to this patient's current scenario.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Agnostic Therapy in Rare Solid Tumors

all_evaluations.explanation: The study provides meaningful clinical evidence for this patient with an SSTR-positive G1 pancreatic NET. Biologically, the patient matches the study population (SSTR+ GEP-NET). Clinically, the patient presents with locally advanced, borderline resectable disease where neoadjuvant PRRT is explicitly being considered to facilitate R0 resection. The study results demonstrate a high Objective Response Rate (ORR) of 56.8% with 212Pb-DOTAMTATE (AlphaMedix) in PRRT-naïve patients, which is significantly higher than standard somatostatin analogs (SSAs) or beta-emitting PRRT (177Lu-DOTATATE). Although the patient has not yet progressed on SSAs (a trial inclusion criterion), the evidence of high tumor shrinkage rates is directly relevant to the clinical goal of downstaging the primary tumor and managing oligometastatic disease. This evidence supports the consideration of Targeted Alpha Therapy as a potent neoadjuvant or systemic option, potentially superior to standard therapies for achieving resectability.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Targeted Alpha-emitter Therapy of PRRT Naïve and Previous PRRT Neuroendocrine Tumor Patients

all_evaluations.explanation: The study is relevant because it evaluates 177Lu-DOTATATE (PRRT) in patients with SSTR-positive, well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors, aligning perfectly with the patient's diagnosis (G1 PanNET, SSTR2-positive). Although the patient currently has stable disease and is being evaluated for potential curative surgery (which was an exclusion criterion for the primary therapy group in the study), the published results provide critical prognostic evidence relevant to treatment planning. Specifically, the study identifies that patients with low liver tumor burden (<50%) and absence of bone metastases or ascites—characteristics matching this patient—have significantly better overall survival and progression-free survival with PRRT. This evidence supports the consideration of PRRT as a highly effective therapeutic option, potentially in the neoadjuvant setting to facilitate R0 resection or as a systemic alternative if surgery is deemed not feasible, helping the tumor board weigh the expected benefit of PRRT against other modalities.
all_evaluations.trial_title: An Open Label Registry Study of Lutetium-177 (DOTA0, TYR3) Octreotate (Lu-DOTA-TATE) Treatment in Patients with Somatostatin Receptor Positive Tumours

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not provide meaningful evidence for this patient's treatment. While the tumor biology (G1 PanNET) aligns, the disease stage and tumor burden are fundamentally discordant. The patient has metastatic (Stage IV), symptomatic disease with a large primary tumor (>4 cm) causing ductal dilation. The study evaluates EUS-guided radiofrequency ablation (RFA) strictly for small (15-25 mm), asymptomatic, localized tumors without metastases. EUS-RFA is a local therapy designed to spare surgery for small incidentalomas; it is not clinically applicable to this patient's large primary tumor (which exceeds safe ablation limits) or her metastatic context, which requires systemic therapy (e.g., SSAs, PRRT) or surgical cytoreduction. Therefore, the study's evidence on ablating small, localized lesions cannot guide therapy for this advanced, metastatic case.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Endoscopic Ultrasound-guided RadioFrequency Ablation for the Treatment Pancreatic NeuroEndocrine Neoplasms

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not provide meaningful evidence for this patient because the provided published results specifically analyze the Biliary Tract Cancer subgroup (cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder carcinoma), which is biologically distinct from the patient's Grade 1 well-differentiated Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumor (PanNET). Although the trial protocol included NETs, the specific efficacy and safety data provided in the input text relate to biliary cancers and cannot be extrapolated to a low-grade PanNET. Furthermore, immunotherapy (Nivolumab plus Ipilimumab) is generally not effective in Grade 1 NETs (which typically have a low mutational burden and 'cold' immune microenvironment) and is not a recommended therapeutic approach when established options like surgery, somatostatin analogs, or PRRT (for which this SSTR-positive patient is a strong candidate) are available.
all_evaluations.trial_title: A Phase II Trial of Ipilimumab and Nivolumab for the Treatment of Rare Cancers

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not meet the criteria for disease alignment or clinical applicability. The patient has a metastatic Grade 1 neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreas (PanNET), whereas the study investigates Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy (SABR) combined with Nivolumab for early-stage (Stage I-IIA) or recurrent Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC). Although the study inclusion criteria mention lung neuroendocrine carcinomas or atypical carcinoids, the primary tumor site (lung vs. pancreas) and disease stage (localized/isolated lung recurrence vs. metastatic liver/nodal disease) are fundamentally different. Furthermore, the treatment modality (lung-directed SABR plus immunotherapy) addresses a clinical scenario—localized lung cancer—that is not present in this patient, who has liver and lymph node metastases without lung involvement. Immunotherapy is also not a standard treatment for G1 PanNETs.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy With or Without Nivolumab in Treating Patients With Stage I-IIA or Recurrent Non-small Cell Lung Cancer

all_evaluations.explanation: The study is not relevant for informing therapy recommendations for this patient. While the disease biology (well-differentiated G1 PanNET) and intervention (Lanreotide) align with the patient's clinical profile, the study fails to meet the criteria for evidence relevance. Specifically, the study (NCT04696042) is an observational investigation focused on Asian populations to confirm the efficacy of Lanreotide in that specific demographic. Without the patient being identified as Asian, this region-specific evidence does not add meaningful value beyond the established global pivotal trials (e.g., CLARINET) that have already defined Lanreotide as a standard of care. Furthermore, the structured input indicates 'No detailed findings available' for the prospective study itself, and the listed publications are either background references or retrospective analyses that predate the study. Consequently, this entry lacks actionable prospective results to guide the complex decision between surgical, neoadjuvant, or systemic approaches for this patient.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Asian Investigation of Lanreotide Autogel® in the Management of GEP-NETs

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not provide meaningful evidence for this patient's current treatment recommendations. First, the clinical context is discordant: the patient has stable disease and is eligible for multiple standard-of-care interventions (surgery, somatostatin analogs, or PRRT given SSTR2 positivity), whereas the study recruits patients with radiological progression who have no possibility of established treatments. Second, the study intervention (Tamoxifen) relies on specific biomarker eligibility (ER/PR expression ≥1%), which is not reported for this patient and is not a standard routine marker for pancreatic NETs. Finally, the study results demonstrated only 'modest antitumor effects' (median PFS 7.9 months), which would not justify prioritizing this experimental hormonal approach over established, highly effective therapies available to this patient in the first-line or neoadjuvant setting.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Study of Tamoxifen in Well Differentiated Neuroendocrine Tumors and Hormone Receptor Positive Expression

all_evaluations.explanation: The study provides meaningful evidence for this patient's disease management. Biologically, the patient's Grade 1 pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (pNET) aligns perfectly with the study's pNET cohort, which enrolled Grade 1-2 patients. Clinically, while the patient currently has stable disease and the study required progressive disease, the results are highly relevant for the inevitable scenario of disease progression (alternative treatment path). The study (Halperin et al., JAMA Oncol 2022) reports a 20% objective response rate and 14.9 months progression-free survival with Atezolizumab plus Bevacizumab. This offers actionable evidence for a non-standard, immune-checkpoint/VEGF inhibitor combination, which is particularly valuable given the general scarcity of immunotherapy data in low-grade NETs. This evidence informs the broader therapeutic strategy, potentially serving as a later-line option after standard treatments (SSAs, PRRT) or if the patient becomes refractory to current therapies.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Atezolizumab and Bevacizumab in Treating Patients With Rare Solid Tumors

all_evaluations.explanation: This study does not currently provide meaningful clinical evidence to guide therapy recommendations because the provided publication is a methodology paper describing the trial design (SORENTO) without reporting efficacy or safety results. While the patient's profile (G1 SSTR-positive metastatic Pan-NET) and the treatment context (first-line Somatostatin Analogues) align perfectly with the study's inclusion criteria, the lack of published outcomes (e.g., PFS, ORR) means there is no data to evaluate the comparative effectiveness of the investigational drug (CAM2029) versus the standard of care. Consequently, Criterion 3 (Evidence Quality and Relevance) is not met.
all_evaluations.trial_title: A Trial to Assess Efficacy and Safety of Octreotide Subcutaneous Depot in Patients with GEP-NET

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not meet the criteria for Evidence Quality and Relevance regarding therapy recommendations. While the patient aligns biologically (NET), the study evaluates the diagnostic yield of 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT in patients with *suspected* but unconfirmed NETs (PMID: 37703482). This patient already has a confirmed diagnosis and has already undergone a comparable SSTR-PET (DOTATOC) which showed intense uptake. Consequently, the study's findings on diagnostic utility do not provide actionable evidence to guide the specific therapeutic decision facing the tumor board (e.g., choosing between upfront resection, neoadjuvant PRRT, or SSAs). The study validates a diagnostic tool the patient has already received but does not offer comparative efficacy or safety data on the treatment modalities under consideration.
all_evaluations.trial_title: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET for Management of Neuroendocrine Tumors

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not meet the criteria for disease alignment or clinical applicability. The patient has a well-differentiated Grade 1 pancreatic NET (Ki-67 2%), whereas the study specifically recruits patients with Grade 3 Neuroendocrine Neoplasms (NEC G3 or NET G3) who have progressed on first-line platinum-based chemotherapy. The biological behavior and standard treatment algorithms for G1 NETs differ significantly from G3 neoplasms; platinum-based chemotherapy is not a standard first-line approach for G1 tumors. Consequently, evidence regarding the safety and efficacy of Everolimus in a post-platinum G3 setting cannot be meaningfully extrapolated to guide therapy for a treatment-naive G1 patient, for whom established evidence (e.g., RADIANT trials) already exists.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Safety and Tolerability of Everolimus as Second-line Treatment in Poorly Differentiated Neuroendocrine Carcinoma / Neuroendocrine Carcinoma G3 (WHO 2010) and Neuroendocrine Tumor G3 - an Investigator Initiated Phase II Study

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not provide meaningful evidence for therapy recommendations because it evaluates a diagnostic tool (AI-assisted EUS) rather than a therapeutic intervention. While the disease biology aligns (pancreatic solid lesions including NETs), the patient already has a confirmed diagnosis via EUS-FNA and DOTATOC PET/CT. The study's published results focus on improving diagnostic accuracy and differentiating lesion types, which does not address the specific clinical question regarding therapeutic management (e.g., surgery vs. neoadjuvant PRRT vs. SSAs) for this patient with established metastatic G1 PanNET. Therefore, the evidence is not applicable to the patient's current need for treatment decision-making.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Artificial Intelligence in EUS for Diagnosing Pancreatic Solid Lesions

all_evaluations.explanation: The study fails the Disease/Biology Alignment and Treatment Context criteria. The patient has a metastatic Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumor (Pan-NET), whereas the study focuses exclusively on Appendiceal Neuroendocrine Tumors (aNETs) measuring 1-2 cm. These are distinct clinical entities with different biological behaviors, staging systems, and surgical guidelines. The study evaluates the necessity of right hemicolectomy versus appendectomy for localized appendiceal disease, which provides no actionable evidence for managing a locally advanced, metastatic pancreatic NET requiring consideration of pancreaticoduodenectomy or systemic therapy. The findings regarding surgical extent in the appendix cannot be extrapolated to the pancreas.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Distant Metastases and Long-Term Survival After Complete Resection of Neuroendocrine Tumors of the Appendix

all_evaluations.explanation: This study provides meaningful evidence for the patient's treatment planning, particularly regarding the potential for Peptide Receptor Radionuclide Therapy (PRRT) to induce tumor shrinkage. Biologically, the patient's SSTR-positive, G1 pancreatic NET aligns perfectly with the study population, which specifically reported high efficacy in the pancreatic NET subgroup (84.6% partial or minor response). Clinically, the patient is symptomatic and presents with locally advanced/borderline resectable disease; the study's inclusion of symptomatic patients and its focus on maximizing tumor absorbed dose to improve response rates is directly relevant to the considered 'neoadjuvant' scenario aimed at downstaging for potential R0 resection. Although the patient currently has stable disease on CT, her symptoms meet the study's 'progressive and/or symptomatic' eligibility criterion. The published results demonstrating significant objective responses and favorable toxicity profiles support the consideration of PRRT (potentially with personalized dosimetry) as a systemic therapy to facilitate future surgical intervention or control symptoms.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Personalized PRRT of Neuroendocrine Tumors

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not provide meaningful evidence to guide therapy for this patient (Criteria 2 and 3 not met). The patient has a well-differentiated G1 pancreatic NET with **stable disease** and is **SSTR2-positive**, making her a candidate for standard therapies like somatostatin analogs (SSAs), surgery, or PRRT. In contrast, the study targets patients with documented disease progression within the last 12 months. Furthermore, the published results (PMID: 36255391) indicate that clinical activity was significantly driven by lung NENs (ORR 64%) compared to non-lung NENs (ORR ~12%), suggesting the Nivolumab plus Temozolomide combination has limited efficacy for pancreatic subtypes. Given the patient's indolent G1 biology and the availability of superior, evidence-based options (SSAs, PRRT), this experimental chemo-immunotherapy regimen is not clinically applicable or competitive with standard of care.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Nivolumab and Temozolomide in Treating Patients With Recurrent or Refractory Small-Cell Lung Cancer or Advanced Neuroendocrine Cancer

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not provide meaningful evidence for this patient because of a fundamental mismatch in disease biology and clinical utility. The patient has a non-functioning pancreatic NET (G1), whereas the study focuses exclusively on validating 5-HIAA (plasma vs. urine) as a biomarker for small-intestine (midgut) NETs. 5-HIAA measures serotonin metabolism, which is relevant for monitoring carcinoid syndrome in midgut tumors but is not a standard marker for non-functioning pancreatic NETs. Additionally, the study is diagnostic/prognostic in nature, aiming to validate a testing method, and offers no therapeutic data to guide the decision between surgery, PRRT, or systemic therapy for this patient's locally advanced/metastatic disease.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Diagnostic Performances of Urine and Plasma 5-hydroxyindolacetic Acid (5HIAA) Values in Patients With Small-intestine Neuroendocrine Tumors

all_evaluations.explanation: The study aligns well with the patient's diagnosis of a well-differentiated pancreatic NET (G1 included in the study population). While the patient currently has stable disease and might be considered for surgery or Somatostatin Analogues (SSAs) first, chemotherapy (e.g., streptozotocin or temozolomide) is a standard option for pancreatic NETs, particularly in neoadjuvant settings to downstage locally advanced tumors (vascular contact) or for future progressive disease. The study provides clinically actionable evidence (PMID: 39586038) demonstrating that MGMT deficiency predicts a significantly higher objective response rate to alkylating agents (52.9% vs 11.5% in proficient tumors), whereas oxaliplatin efficacy is independent of MGMT status. This evidence is highly relevant for the tumor board when discussing neoadjuvant strategies or selecting the most effective systemic chemotherapy regimen should the patient require cytoreduction.
all_evaluations.trial_title: MGMT-NET: O6-methylguanine-DNA Methyltransferase (MGMT) Status in Neuroendocrine Tumors: Predictive Factor of Response to Alkylating Agents

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not meet the criteria for Disease/Biology Alignment or Evidence Relevance. The patient has a well-differentiated Grade 1 pancreatic NET (Ki-67 2%), a biologically indolent tumor type. In contrast, the study's neuroendocrine cohort specifically targets aggressive histologies, including Neuroendocrine Carcinomas (NECs) and Grade 3 NETs, explicitly excluding the patient's low-grade disease. Biologically, G1 NETs are distinct from NECs/G3 NETs and typically do not respond to checkpoint inhibitors (Nivolumab/Ipilimumab) due to a low tumor mutational burden and 'cold' immune microenvironment. Furthermore, the provided published results (PMID: 40608313) report outcomes exclusively for the gynecological clear cell carcinoma cohort, offering no efficacy or safety data relevant to neuroendocrine neoplasms. Consequently, this study provides no applicable evidence to guide therapy for a patient with a G1 NET.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Combination Immunotherapy in Rare Cancers Under InvesTigation
